Fire/flames and snakes suggest trauma content not represented anywhere in the memory or appraisal items and not plausibly linked to partner physical abuse unless there were specific undisclosed trauma details. The rest of the profile centers on bodily pain, terror, injustice, contamination, and identity change following interpersonal assault, so these two triggers appear clinically incoherent with the formulation and with the other selected items.

vignette:
Nnamdi was a 30-year-old African American man who worked as a curriculum designer and lived alone in a small apartment where he spent much of his time drafting lesson plans on his laptop, reviewing materials, and joining meetings from the same kitchen table. He had come to treatment after months of feeling increasingly unlike himself since a relationship that had ended badly and violently. In the early stages, he had tried to frame it as something he should simply move past, but what happened with his former partner had stayed with him in a way that felt raw and embodied. During one argument in her apartment, she had turned physically abusive, and the details of that night remained difficult for him to recount without becoming visibly tense. He remembered the feeling of being trapped in the space, the shock of being hurt by someone he had trusted, and how quickly fear had taken over. Even now, when the memory came back, it did not feel like an ordinary recollection. He described the same terror returning with it, sudden and immediate, as though he were back in that room rather than thinking about it from a distance.

In the months after the breakup, Nnamdi noticed that certain everyday experiences pulled him sharply back toward that night. If he passed someone on the street or in his building who smelled of alcohol, his body would stiffen before he had fully registered why. The smell seemed to do something immediate and unpleasant, as though it bypassed his thinking and brought the whole scene forward at once. He was also unsettled by burnt smells, especially when something scorched in the kitchen or drifted in from a neighbor's apartment. At home, he might be preparing dinner for himself when a pan was left too long on the stove, and the faint burnt odor would stop him in place. In those moments, he became acutely aware of his body, and the memory would sometimes bring back not only the terror but a striking sense of physical pain in the same parts of his body that had hurt during the assault. He described this with quiet disbelief, as though it was hard to understand how remembering could produce pain that felt so closely matched to what had happened. He also noticed that the memory itself could carry smells with it. When he thought about the event, there were times when he could almost smell the alcohol or the burnt odor again, which made the memory feel less like a thought and more like a brief return to the scene.

As time went on, Nnamdi found himself making sense of what had happened in ways that were painful and uncompromising. He said that the person he had become was unrecognisable to him. Before the assault, he had seen himself as composed, reliable, and easy to be around, someone who managed his work well and moved through life with a steady confidence. Now he felt altered in a way he did not recognize, more guarded and distant, and he struggled to reconcile that with who he had once believed himself to be. What happened to him also felt deeply unfair to him. He spoke with a clear sense that nothing had been done about it, that the harm had been allowed to stand without consequence, and that this added to his distress. He was not describing dramatic public action or a legal process that had failed; rather, there was a private sense of injustice that remained unresolved in him, as if the event had left him carrying something that should never have been his to bear. Alongside that, he felt dirty or contaminated because of what had happened, and he said this with visible shame, as though the assault had left a stain on him that no amount of bathing or time could wash away.

His work as a curriculum designer remained important to him, but it had become more difficult to inhabit fully. In meetings, if someone made a casual remark about family or asked about family plans, he felt a sudden tightening that was hard to explain and could leave him wanting to withdraw. He was single and had become increasingly private about his personal life, partly because these comments seemed to bring him back to the loss and humiliation tied to the relationship he had tried to leave behind. At home and at work, he often tried to manage these reactions by staying busy, keeping interactions brief, and avoiding situations in which the alcohol smell or burnt odor might catch him off guard. Over time, he noticed how much effort this took and how narrowed his life had become. He eventually sought help because he was tired of feeling as though parts of his own body and mind were no longer his, and because the memories could still arrive with such force that he feared being overwhelmed by them. What he most hoped for was some way to feel recognizable to himself again, and what he most feared was that the event had changed him permanently.
